newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Nov 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Nov 7.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- RISK TO STATUS OF CONVERTED SOCIETIES

Treasury Minister Angela Knight has unveiled a newly drafted Building Societies Bill that would mean societies that convert and then make an acquisition will lose their five-year protection from takeover. The Halifax, which is planning to convert next summer, has decided it does not need the protection when it floats, but the Alliance and Leicester, Woolwich and Northern Rock are expected to take full advantage of the five- year protection allowed under the current law.
-- MP CHIDES WALLIS ON WINDFALL TAX

Chairman of PowerGen, Ed Wallis, told MPs at a Commons Trade and Industry committee he believed the electricity generator could escape the windfall profits tax on privatised utilities planned by the Labour Party if it won the next general election. A spokesman for Mr Blair denied any decision had been made about which utilities would be covered by the tax. Mr Wallis warned that if the company was included it would limit investment and put jobs at risk.
-- THREE OIL GROUPS POOL UK REFINING AND SALES

Gulf, Elf and Murco are planning to merge their British refining and marketing operations to create the fourth largest force in the forecourts. This will involve closing Gulf's Milford Haven refinery. The three companies expect to save 50 million stg a year by forming one company to run 1,500 service stations. Wood Mackenzie Consultants estimate the merged company will have a market share of about eight percent, putting it behind Esso, Shell and BP /Mobile.
THE TIMES
-- BANK DEMANDS FURTHER RATE CUT

The Bank of England has dashed Tory hopes of a "pre-emptive" increase in base rates announced by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke with a strong demand for higher interest rates. This will assure a period of stable mortgage rates and keep monetary policy off the pre-election agenda. A Bank of England report said the quarter-point increase last week in base rates was not enough to ensure inflation would fall below the Government's 2.5 percent target increase.
-- BARINGS SUES FORMER CHIEF OVER LOAN

Ron Baker, the former head of derivatives at Barings who left after the Nick Leeson scandal, is being sued by the bank to recover a 100,000-stg loan he allegedly failed to repay. The bank gave loans to directors and employees at commercial rates. Barings claim that under the terms of the loan, Mr Baker was supposed to pay it back at the end of June last year. It says he was reminded to pay a week before the due date and again at the end of September last year but refused to pay on both occasions.
-- US UTILITY PUTS EAST MIDLANDS ON BID ALERT

East Midlands Electricity, one of five remaining independent regional companies, is on bid alert after a potential American predator admitted interest. Dominion Resources of Virginia have said they were interested in the company after a huge jump in share price. East Midlands said that until there was something concrete from Dominion it could not comment. East Midland is thought likely to defend a bid.
THE GUARDIAN
-- USAIR TO BUY AIRBUS FLEET

Airbus Industrie has made a 11.25 billion-stg agreement to supply up to 400 aircraft to modernise USAir's fleet. This is one of the world's biggest ever orders. British Aerospace will be one of the main beneficiaries of the deal because it has a 20 percent share in the European consortium and builds Airbus wings. It will create thousands of jobs. Rolls-Royce is also competing to supply the engines. Airbus has fought off fierce competition from Boeing to secure the order.
-- OFTEL WARNS BT ON MURDOCH CONNECTION

Don Cruickshank, the telecom regulator, has said he will object to British Telecom becoming a large shareholder in Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. He is concerned about regulation of the converging telecommunications and information industries. He says the new communications industry will be all distribution and sale of information in digital form and the old boundaries will fall away. Oftel will make its views on the purchase of MCI known to the authorities when the formal investigations begin.
-- TWO RIVAL EMAP DIRECTORS TAKE BATTLE TO CHAIRMAN

Two rebel directors of Emap, Ken Simmonds and Joe Cooke, have publically accused the media group's chairman, Sir John Hoskyns, of misleading shareholders before this summer's annual meeting. The pair say Hoskyns wanted to oust them because they opposed controversial changes to Emap's articles of association at the meeting. They say Hoskyns had promised institution investors that the changes, which make it easier for Emap to remove directors, would not be used against them.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CLINTON TEAM TELLS OF US UTILITY CONCERNS OVER WINDFALL TAX

The Clinton adminstration has approached Labour leader Tony Blair's office with concerns over the windfall tax being imposed on US utilities that have acquired British regional electricity companies in the last 18 months. Three British RECs have so far been taken over by US utilities at a cost of 4.4 billion stg, and two others are close to being purchased, putting nearly half of the UK electricity distribution industry in US hands.
-- CBI HEAD BACKS TOUGH SCHOOL DISCIPLINE

Director general of the Confederation of British Industry, Adair Turner, has suggested that army style discipline should be used in Britain's schools to restore order, and that pupils should wear uniforms. He stressed that his were personal views and not that of the CBI, and said his gut feeling was that a discipline problem did exist which was effecting morale and educational standards.
-- COMPANIES WITH VAT CLAIMS RUSH TO BEAT BUDGET

The prospect of Chancellor Kenneth Clarke introducing legislation designed to limit payouts has led to businesses rushing to make value added tax refund claims ahead of the Budget. This is being fuelled by a court battle between Customs and Excise and six organisations over claims going back several years that Customs claims are not valid. Due to the VAT Tribunal being unable to order Customs to pay the money, companies are being urged to issue writs for the sums owed them.
